fullName: Atomic: a beamline for extremely high-resolution coherent imaging of atomistic structures (Bragg coherent diffraction imaging, 34-ID-F)

status2026.detail: On the APS 'Beamline Commissioning Progress' chart dated 2026-10-05, '34-ID-F: ATOMIC XSD' sits at stage 5 of 6 ('Scientific Commissioning and Early Experiments'), not yet stage 6 ('Restart of General User Program'). The APS Proposal Types page (dated 2026-10-07) already lists 34-ID-F among beamlines taking General User and Rapid Access proposals, so general-user operation is expected to follow. History: a Dec 2021 user town hall covered the timing and scope of 34-ID construction; the Dec 2023 plan was scientific commissioning in cycle 2025-1; Dec 2024/Jan 2025 updates said only 'infrastructure' for Atomic/3DMN would be in place when the project closed in mid-2025; Aug 2025 update expected first light in October 2025 and first users late in run 2026-1; the Oct 2025 update reported Atomic moved into commissioning ('all of the feature beamlines are now online'); the 2026-01-26 chart showed stage 4, technical commissioning. MEDSI 2025 states all nine feature beamlines met their Key Performance Parameters. Stale pages: the Beamline Directory status field still reads 'Construction' and the Feature Beamlines page still says 'Atomic (to come)'. No peer-reviewed post-upgrade ATOMIC result was found as of 2026-10-09; 2026 science highlights crediting '34-ID-C' appear to report pre-upgrade data. Project context: the January 2026 update said the upgrade had 'all scope delivered', and the APS-U project received final approval (CD-4) in January 2026; the MEDSI 2025 KPPs were brightness at a defined energy plus verification of the usable energy range (only ISN had a spot-size KPP), so meeting them does not demonstrate the 50 nm zoom spot.

tagline: A lens-free X-ray microscope that rebuilds single nanocrystals in 3D and reveals the strain hidden inside them.
plainSummary: ATOMIC, at the far end of beamline 34-ID, makes 3D pictures of the inside of single crystals, each smaller than a bacterium: specks of battery material, catalyst particles, grains of metal. It has no imaging lens. Instead, a laser-like ('coherent') X-ray beam strikes one crystal at exactly the angle at which its rows of atoms reflect, and a camera up to a few metres away records the speckled pattern that bounces off. A computer works backwards from the speckles to rebuild the crystal in 3D, showing not only its shape but where its atomic layers are squeezed, stretched or broken: the hidden strain and defects that decide whether a battery lasts or a metal cracks. The upgraded APS makes hundreds of times more of this laser-like light, and a 'zoom lens' of bendable mirrors is designed to shrink the spot from 2 micrometres to 50 nanometres to match each crystal. In October 2026 ATOMIC is in scientific commissioning, running its first experiments.
expertSummary: ATOMIC (34-ID-F) is the APS-U feature beamline dedicated to Bragg coherent diffractive imaging (BCDI) and related coherent methods, succeeding the 34-ID-C BCDI program where 3D strain imaging inside a nanocrystal was first demonstrated (Pfeifer et al. 2006). It takes the inboard branch of the canted 34-ID straight: a downstream revolver undulator (21/25 mm periods, ~2.1 m) canted 1 mrad from the 3DMN U28; a windowless CUFE with a 2 × 2 mm² exit aperture per branch; a flat Si/Rh/Pt three-stripe white-beam mirror at 3.0 mrad (31.3 m) deflecting inboard; a coherence-defining slit pair (26.8 m and 50.3 m); a ~1.1 mm small-offset, horizontally deflecting Si(111) DCM (5.3-30 keV) with pink-beam bypass; and a two-stage bendable 'zoom' KB system (KB1 ~54 m in 34-ID-C, KB2 ~15 m downstream in 34-ID-F) that varies the final numerical aperture to give 50 nm-2 µm spots (FDR Sec. 4-9.3 still says 50 nm-1.5 µm) at a fixed focal plane with ~50 mm working distance. FDR ray traces predict 3.1 × 10¹² ph/s/0.1%BW into 50 nm (4.6 × 10¹² into 2 µm) at 8.7 keV in brightness mode; KB figure errors must stay below 1 nm rms. The FDR endstation comprises a beam pre-conditioning platform, a sample-positioning diffractometer and a separate detector-positioning diffractometer (arm ~4.5 m in design drawings), supports pink-beam Laue orientation for multi-reflection strain-tensor BCDI, and operando cells (RT-900 °C gas, ~80 K cryo, liquid flow, coin cells). Design target: ≤1 nm resolution versus ~10-30 nm typical pre-upgrade BCDI. Status: scientific commissioning/early experiments (5 Oct 2026).

whatAPSUEnables.plain: Coherent imaging only works with the part of an X-ray beam whose waves march in step, and on the old APS that was a tiny fraction of the light - like trying to see interference with a flashlight instead of a laser pointer. The new storage ring squeezes the electron beam about 19 times narrower sideways, so far more of the X-rays are 'laser-like'. ATOMIC is designed to pour hundreds of times more useful light into a spot only 50 nanometres wide, which is expected to cut some 3D strain pictures to tens of seconds rather than the several minutes typical before the upgrade, follow batteries and catalysts while they work, and push toward pictures fine enough to show atomic-scale distortions.
whatAPSUEnables.expert: The MBA lattice cuts the horizontal source size from 280 to 14.7 µm rms (brightness mode), raising the coherent fraction at ~10 keV from ~0.04% to ~5% (derived) and the coherent flux at 20 keV ~500-fold (3.1 × 10¹³ vs 6 × 10¹⁰ ph/s, FDR Table 1.1, for an ID optimized for 20 keV rather than ATOMIC's revolver). ATOMIC exploits this with (i) slit-based coherent-mode selection (S1 at 26.8 m, S2 at 50.3 m) instead of the heavy horizontal aperturing needed before (pre-upgrade 34-ID-C slitted the beam to ~30 × 70 µm before its KB), (ii) a zoom KB that matches beam size to sample (50 nm-2 µm) so nearly the whole coherent flux lands on the crystal (3.1 × 10¹² ph/s/0.1%BW in 50 nm at 8.7 keV), giving flux densities approaching ~2 × 10⁹ ph/s/nm² (PDR), and (iii) higher design energies (to 30 keV) for penetrating operando cells and diamond-anvil environments (derived caveat: at the FDR 3.0 mrad grazing angle the Pt stripe's critical energy is ~28 keV, so throughput near 30 keV through the white-beam mirror plus four KB mirrors will be low unless angles are reduced; not yet reported from commissioning). The PDR estimated that ~10¹⁸ ph/µm² (Dietze & Shpyrko) needed for 3D atomic-resolution imaging of a ~20 nm Au crystal could be accumulated in ~1000 s at 4.9 × 10¹² ph/s into 50 nm, and sub-10-nm operando imaging in tens of seconds. Consequences: detectors (flux per pixel), sample heating (~8 mW in a 50 × 50 nm² spot at 10 keV, PDR), radiation damage, and a ~400× jump in data volume (250-300 TB/yr) become first-order design problems.
quantitative: Time per 3D BCDI dataset: several minutes at third-generation sources (e.g. ~2 min per operando 3D scan at 34-ID-C) vs sub-10-nm operando imaging expected in tens of seconds at APS-U (PDR estimate)

Coherent flux at 20 keV: 3.12 × 10¹³ ph/s (APS-U brightness mode) vs 6 × 10¹⁰ ph/s (pre-upgrade APS), factor ~520; FDR quotes 'a factor of 540 at 20 keV' Note: Table 1.1 values are for an ID optimized for 20 keV, not ATOMIC's 2.1 m revolver; at ATOMIC's ~9 keV the gain is smaller (derived coherent-fraction gain ~125× at 10 keV, times ~2-3× more central-cone flux).
Horizontal source size 14.7 µm rms vs 280 µm rms pre-upgrade (19× smaller); horizontal divergence 2.8 vs 11.6 µrad

Coherent fraction at 10 keV, brightness mode, 2.1 m undulator: ~5% (fx ~0.11, fy ~0.48) vs ~0.04% pre-upgrade (derived here from the FDR Table 1.1 source parameters with σr = √(2 λ L)/4π, σr' = √(λ/2L))

Focal spot range 50 nm - 2 µm (simulated 47 × 50 nm² to 2.1 × 2.1 µm² at 8.7 keV) vs ~0.5 × 0.7 µm (H × V) typical at pre-upgrade 34-ID-C: ~140× smaller spot area at the small end

techniques.name: Bragg coherent diffractive imaging
techniques.plain: A coherent X-ray beam hits one small crystal set at exactly the right angle to reflect. The reflected X-rays form a 3D speckle pattern; rocking the crystal through a tiny angle records it slice by slice. A computer recovers the missing phases and rebuilds the crystal in 3D, with colours that show where its atomic layers are pushed or pulled.
techniques.expert: Isolated crystal (tens of nm to ~1-2 µm) fully illuminated by a coherent, ideally size-matched beam; 3D intensity around one reflection G_hkl is sampled by a rocking scan (typ. tens of 2D frames over a fraction of a degree, e.g. 76 frames × 1 s over ±0.3° at 34-ID-C) with oversampling ≥2 per dimension; iterative phase retrieval (ER/HIO with shrink-wrap, genetic/population schemes; cohere package; AutoPhaseNN initial guesses) gives a complex density ρ(r)e^{i φ(r)} with φ = G·u(r). Displacement sensitivity is a small fraction of d_hkl (sub-ångström), strain ~10⁻⁴; pre-upgrade 3D resolution 10-30 nm; the APS-U design target is ≤1 nm. Review of the method: Robinson & Harder 2009. Fringe spacing scales with λ, so at higher energies speckles compress on the detector; 'unbinning' phase retrieval was demonstrated at 34-ID-C by emulating 45 keV with 15 keV and a 3× shorter detector distance (Maddali et al. 2019).

techniques.name: Laue-assisted multi-reflection BCDI (full strain tensor)
techniques.plain: First a rainbow ('pink') X-ray beam makes many reflections at once, which tells the scientists exactly how the crystal is oriented. Then they switch to a single colour and measure three or more different reflections from the same crystal, so they can map stretching and twisting in every direction.
techniques.expert: Pink-beam Laue patterns recorded on a detector ~25 mm from the sample (at 34-ID-C an ASI Quad Timepix GaAs detector at 26 mm in Pateras et al. 2020, an Eiger2 500K at ~25 mm in Zhang et al. 2023) are indexed (LaueGo) to get the orientation matrix of an arbitrarily oriented sub-µm crystal; the mono beam (heated second DCM crystal keeps mono and pink beams coincident through the focusing optics) is then used to collect BCDI at ≥3 non-coplanar reflections, from which the six-component strain tensor is reconstructed. The FDR keeps pink-beam bypass on the ATOMIC HDCM for this workflow and defines a 'Pink Beam CDI mode'; the directory lists Laue orientation analysis as a special capability.

techniques.name: Bragg ptychography (scanning BCDI)
techniques.plain: For crystals or films bigger than the beam, the beam is stepped across the sample in overlapping spots and all the speckle patterns are combined, like stitching a panorama, to image strain over a larger area.
techniques.expert: Planned for samples larger than the ~1.5-2 µm maximum zoom spot; overlapping illumination positions provide redundancy to recover both probe and object; phase-retrieval needs shared with PtychoProbe/ISN. Zoom KB lets the probe size be optimised for the field of view vs. scan overhead. Not yet documented as a commissioned mode at 34-ID-F.

techniques.name: Atomic-resolution (wide-angle) coherent diffractive imaging
techniques.plain: The long-term dream behind the beamline's name: measure the faint speckles far out from the main reflection (or from non-crystalline samples) to see arrangements of individual atoms in 3D.
techniques.expert: Requires measuring to q ~ 1 Å⁻¹ and beyond with enormous dynamic range (intensity ~q⁻⁴) and doses ~10¹⁷–10¹⁸ ph/µm² (amorphous vs crystalline Au, Dietze & Shpyrko); PDR/Early-Science example: Cu64Zr36 metallic-glass nanopillar (20 nm × 50 nm), qmax = 1.26 Å⁻¹, 2 × 10¹² ph/s into 20 × 26 nm² → ~7 min per view, ~1 h for a ~10-view tomographic set per strain state. Aspirational; not demonstrated at ATOMIC as of 2026. The 2016 proposal (WP28) framed the goal as pushing coherent imaging 'toward atomic resolution in both crystalline and amorphous materials'.

techniques.name: Polychromatic / pink-beam coherent imaging
techniques.plain: Using a broader band of X-ray colours at once gives many more photons, useful for weakly scattering samples or for fast imaging without rocking the crystal.
techniques.expert: FDR 'Pink Beam CDI mode' delivers focused pink beam to the endstation; PDR anticipated using up to ~10 spatial modes or a full harmonic bandwidth with modal/polychromatic phase retrieval, and broadband 3D imaging without sample rotation. Undulator harmonic bandwidth and KB chromatic acceptance (mirrors are achromatic) make this possible; status at 34-ID-F unknown.

techniques.name: Operando / in situ BCDI with AI-accelerated phase retrieval
techniques.plain: Crystals are imaged inside working batteries, gas-flow catalysis cells, heaters, coolers or liquids, and neural networks turn the data into 3D images fast enough to steer the experiment.
techniques.expert: Directory equipment: heating chamber with gas flow (RT-900 °C), cryo chamber (to ~80 K), RT liquid flow cell with peristaltic pump, RGA, coin-cell holder with BioLogic SP300. ~50 mm working distance (FDR) leaves room for cells. Software: cohere (ER/HIO, GPU via ArrayFire/CuPy) with AutoPhaseNN initialisation; physics-aware CNN + automatic-differentiation refinement (3D-CDI-NN predicts structure and strain hundreds of times faster than iterative phase retrieval, per the published abstract; AutoPhaseNN ~100× faster once trained per Yao et al. 2022, '>10×' in the 2024 computing strategy). PDR also planned resonant/anomalous and dichroic BCDI (diamond phase plate), not carried into the FDR.

scienceCases.title: Watching batteries break (and heal) from the inside
scienceCases.plain: Battery electrodes are made of tiny crystals that swell and shrink every time the battery charges. BCDI has watched defects called dislocations appear, move and vanish inside single particles of working batteries. ATOMIC's brighter, smaller beam should make these movies sharper and faster.
scienceCases.expert: Operando BCDI at APS imaged dislocation dynamics in LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 spinel nanoparticles during charge (Ulvestad et al., Science 2015), metastable screw-dislocation loops at antiphase boundaries in Na-ion layered oxides (Gorobtsov et al. 2023, 34-ID-C), defects in garnet LLZO solid electrolyte grains (Sun et al. 2021, 34-ID-C) and the operando phase-transformation front in LNMO (9 keV, 800 nm focus, ~2 min per 3D scan; Sun et al. arXiv 2023, 34-ID-C). Coherent multi-crystal diffraction at 34-ID-C also tracked asynchronous domain dynamics inside NMC cathode particles (Xue et al. 2023). APS-U coherent flux and the 50 nm zoom spot target sub-10-nm operando imaging in tens of seconds (PDR).

scienceCases.title: Seeing where catalysts work
scienceCases.plain: Catalyst particles speed up chemical reactions mostly at their corners and edges. BCDI can see the atomic layers near those spots stretch as molecules stick and react - like seeing a muscle twitch where it is working.
scienceCases.expert: BCDI of ~300 nm Au crystals during ascorbic-acid decomposition showed strain concentrating at corners, explained by reactive MD as chemisorbed hydroxyl (Ulvestad et al., arXiv 2016; PDR Fig. 6.1b). PDR flagship experiment: image an Ag-Au alloy nanocrystal, follow operando electrochemical dealloying with anomalous CDI near the Au L3 edge (~12 keV), then catalysis and coarsening of the resulting nanoporous gold - using the zoom optics to repeat on crystals of different sizes.

scienceCases.title: Defects in tough metals for fusion and aerospace
scienceCases.plain: Strong metals are full of microscopic flaws. Scientists cut tiny crystals out of real engineering parts and use BCDI to measure how each flaw bends the surrounding atoms, helping design metals that survive heat and radiation.
scienceCases.expert: Hofmann et al. (2020) located specific dislocations in tungsten by Laue microdiffraction (34-ID-E), extracted micro-crystals by FIB with damage-minimising preparation and imaged the full strain tensor by BCDI at 34-ID-C. Related APS work by the same group with 34-ID-C staff: annealing of FIB damage in Au microcrystals (Yang et al., J. Synchrotron Rad. 2021) and in situ corrosion of a Co-Fe microcrystal at 34-ID-C (Yang et al., CrystEngComm 2022; 740 × 680 nm beam at 9 keV, BCDI 3D resolution 10-30 nm, strain ~2 × 10⁻⁴); a dislocation loop annihilating into a grain boundary at ~400 °C in a heated polycrystalline Au film, imaged with 10 nm spatial and sub-angstrom displacement resolution (Yau et al., Science 2017; APS, station not stated in the sources checked). ATOMIC adds in-situ Laue orientation and a size-matched beam for grains embedded in films.

scienceCases.title: How crystals grow - clues frozen in strain
scienceCases.plain: When minerals grow from water, impurities and the growth path leave strain locked inside. Mapping that strain in single crystals tells geochemists whether a crystal grew atom-by-atom or from clumps of precursors.
scienceCases.expert: BCDI at 34-ID-C during growth of calcite and barite with/without Sr2+ showed high defect density and preserved lattice strain in calcite consistent with nonclassical growth (prenucleation clusters/amorphous precursors) versus classical growth in barite, corroborated by HRTEM and MD (Yuan et al., JACS 2026).

scienceCases.title: Atom-by-atom failure in metallic glass (aspirational)
scienceCases.plain: Metallic glasses are super-strong metals with no crystal order that fail suddenly. The dream is to image the actual atoms rearranging just before a tiny glass pillar yields.
scienceCases.expert: PDR/Early-Science feasibility: Cu64Zr36 nanopillar (20 nm diameter), MD model of 96,000 atoms, patterns to qmax = 1.26 Å⁻¹ with 10¹³ ph/nm² give 0.1 Å position precision; with ~2 × 10¹² ph/s (0.01% BW) focused into 20 × 26 nm², ~7 min per dataset and ~1 h per strain state for ~10 orientations. Dietze & Shpyrko: amorphous samples need ~10× less dose (~10¹⁷ ph/µm²) than crystalline ones for atomic resolution.

scienceCases.title: Spin-lattice coupling in quantum materials (planned)
scienceCases.plain: In some exotic oxides the magnetism and the crystal lattice are tightly linked. Polarization-controlled coherent imaging could show how defects disturb the magnetic patterns.
scienceCases.expert: PDR proposed atomic-scale resonant BCDI of Sr2IrO4 antiferromagnetic twin domains across temperature and field with controllable polarization (diamond phase plate, circular polarization to ~12 keV), and dichroic BCDI of magnetic systems. The FDR does not list a phase plate, so this remains a future option.

scienceCases.title: Imaging at the speed of the experiment
scienceCases.plain: ATOMIC will make data hundreds of times faster than before, so Argonne trains neural networks that turn speckle patterns into 3D pictures in seconds, letting scientists decide on the fly what to measure next.
scienceCases.expert: Expected 250-300 TB/yr (fast BCDI ~20 MB/s written; high-resolution CDI frames ~61 MB) vs 0.65 TB/yr at 34-ID-C; cohere with multi-GPU distributed FFTs (with ALCF/NVIDIA), AutoPhaseNN (>10× faster than iterative per the 2024 strategy; ~100× once trained per Yao et al. 2022), physics-aware 3D-CDI-NN + AD refinement, MD-library-informed reconstructions (LDRD 'A.I. C.D.I.'). AI is also used to align the nanofocusing mirrors (AutoFocus: developed on a digital twin of the 34-ID-C bendable KB, then validated experimentally on a similar KB system at 28-ID-B).

insertionDevices.name: ATOMIC revolver undulator - 21 mm array (APS21R25#8S, magnet structure APS21#13S)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (two magnet structures on a rotating strongback, common 4-motor gap separation mechanism)
insertionDevices.notes: Downstream device of the 34-ID straight → inboard canted beam (FDR Table 4.62). As installed: 98 periods, device min gap 8.5 mm, K_eff 1.38, E1 = 8.33 keV at min gap (tunable up to ~16 keV as K→0), Ptot 4.8 kW, peak 190 kW/mrad² at 200 mA. 3rd harmonic covers ~25 keV and above for the 30 keV end of the range (derived). FDR max power through the 2 × 2 mm² mask at 30 m: 763/738 W for the two arrays (pairing of values to arrays ambiguous in FDR Table 4.62). '*' in the ID table marks it a short device; the Beamline Directory quotes 2.3 m (likely overall length). ID table gap limits for S34 DS: device minimum 8.5 mm, administrative minimum 8.65 mm, user minimum 9.0 mm; the tabulated K/E1 are at 8.5 mm, so at the 9.0 mm user minimum E1 is slightly higher (~8.9-9.1 keV for U21, ~5.0-5.1 keV for U25, derived from Halbach-type hybrid field scaling; consistent with the 5.3 keV lower limit).

insertionDevices.name: ATOMIC revolver undulator - 25 mm array (same device, APS25#10S)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (alternate magnet structure)
insertionDevices.notes: Same physical device as above; only one array is active at a time (rotate with gap open). 82 periods, K_eff 1.99, E1 = 4.59 keV at min gap, Ptot 7.0 kW, 196 kW/mrad². Provides the low end of the 5.3-30 keV range. FDR revolver description: Sec. 3-3.3.2.

insertionDevices.name: Partner device (feeds 3DMN, not ATOMIC): U28 planar undulator APS28#13S
insertionDevices.notes: Upstream device of the same straight → outboard beam to 3DMN; 74 periods, K 2.48, E1 3.00 keV. Listed for context of the canted pair.

source.canting: Two undulators canted by 1.0 mrad in the 34-ID straight, using electromagnetic canting magnets of 0.5 / 1.0 / 0.5 mrad (upstream / centre / downstream) plus a corrector in the middle (FDR Ch. 3 Table 3.20 and ID configuration table); ATOMIC uses the DOWNSTREAM revolver and the INBOARD beam, 3DMN the upstream U28 and the outboard beam. At the 25.4 m exit mask the two 2 × 2 mm² apertures are ~25 mm apart (1 mrad × 25.4 m, derived). Pre-upgrade the coherent-imaging station 34-ID-C used the outboard beam from the upstream undulator and 34-ID-E the inboard beam - the assignment is now reversed.
source.frontEnd: Canted Undulator Front End (CUFE) rated 2 × 10 kW total and 280 kW/mrad² peak power density, windowless (differential-pump) exit for 34-ID. APS-U CUFE features: permanent-magnet clearing magnet upstream of the low-power photon shutter (LPPS), Storage Ring Valve, Burn-Through Fixed Mask 1, fixed masks (upstream mask at 19.4 m designed for up to 418 W/mm² - an FDR design case for an SCU source, not ATOMIC's revolver), GRID fluorescence XBPM1 plus XBPM2 integrated in the exit mask, photon and safety shutters (SS1/SS2). Exit table in 34-ID-A: exit mask at 25.4 m with two 2 × 2 mm² apertures, W exit collimator 2 × (5 × 5 mm²) at 26.1 m.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at the ID (FDR Table 1.1): brightness mode (324 bunches, 42 pm) σx = 14.7 µm, σy = 3.2 µm, σx' = 2.8 µrad, σy' = 1.3 µrad; timing mode (48 bunches, 32 pm) 12.9 / 8.8 µm and 2.5 / 3.7 µrad; pre-upgrade APS 280 / 10.0 µm and 11.6 / 3.4 µrad. Photon source for the 2.1 m revolver at 8.7 keV (derived, Gaussian single-electron terms): Σx ~14.8 µm, Σy ~3.8 µm, Σx' ~6.5 µrad, Σy' ~6.0 µrad (brightness mode), i.e. coherent fractions ~12% (H) and ~51% (V), ~6% total. Caveat: the canted source points sit ~1 m downstream of the straight centre where the beta functions differ slightly from the Table 1.1 values.

branches.name: ATOMIC (inboard canted branch, 34-ID-F)
branches.description: Single-branch coherent-imaging beamline: white-beam slit S1 and mirror in 34-ID-A, shielded transport and masks through 34-ID-B, BPM/slit S2/DCM/zoom KB1/shutter in 34-ID-C, shielded pipe through the 3DMN hutch 34-ID-E, and the endstation (KB2, diffractometers, detectors) in the new 34-ID-F.

branches.name: 3DMN (outboard canted branch, 34-ID-E) - partner
branches.description: Context only (3DMN has its own exhibit). U28 (upstream undulator) → shared CUFE and 34-ID-A FOE → outboard flat mirror at 29.6 m → masks in 34-ID-B → HDCM in 34-ID-C (53.8 m) → micro- (~60 m) and nano-diffraction (~65.5 m) stations in 34-ID-E. Components marked branch null are shared.

components.name: U28 planar undulator (upstream device, feeds 3DMN) - partner
components.distanceNote: Upstream device of the same straight, centre ~-1.2 m from the straight centre (approx., as in the 3DMN exhibit).
components.plain: The first undulator in the same straight section feeds 3DMN, ATOMIC's twin beamline, which maps crystal grains in 3D with a rainbow X-ray beam. Its beam leaves 1 milliradian outboard of ATOMIC's.
components.expert: APS28#13S planar HPMU: 74 × 28 mm periods, K 2.48, E1 3.00 keV at the 8.5 mm minimum gap; outboard canted beam (FDR Table 4.62; ID table). Context only; see the 3DMN exhibit.

components.name: Canting magnets (1 mrad)
components.distanceNote: Centre magnet at the straight centre (0 m, the distance reference); 0.5 mrad magnets at both ends of the straight (~±2.45 m, approx.). Not tabulated in FDR Sec. 4-9.
components.plain: Three small steering magnets kink the electron path by just 1 milliradian (0.06 degrees) between the two undulators of this straight section. Their two X-ray beams drift apart, so one source slot feeds two beamlines: ATOMIC and its twin, 3DMN.
components.expert: Canted geometry with 1 mrad between the two ID beams; electromagnetic canting magnets of 0.5 / 1.0 / 0.5 mrad (upstream / centre / downstream) with a corrector in the middle (FDR Ch. 3 Table 3.20; ID configuration table for 34-ID: 'Planar 2.8 / Rev 2.5/2.1, canting magnets, corrector').

components.name: Revolver undulator U21/U25 (downstream device, inboard beam)
components.distanceNote: Distances in this exhibit are measured from the centre of the 34-ID straight section (the PDR's definition of 'source'; FDR Table 4.63 lists distances 'from source'). The revolver is the downstream device: its centre sits ~1.2 m downstream of the straight centre (approx., as in the 3DMN exhibit), which may explain ~1 m offsets between the FDR component table/drawings and the FDR ray-trace (see the zoom-KB notes).
components.plain: ATOMIC's X-ray source: rows of alternating magnets that make the ring's electrons wiggle and shine an intense, narrow X-ray beam. It is a 'revolver': each jaw carries two magnet rows, one repeating every 21 mm and one every 25 mm, and turns like a revolver's cylinder to swap them for higher or lower X-ray energies.
components.expert: Planar HPMU revolver, 21 mm (98 periods, K 1.38, E1 8.33 keV at 8.5 mm gap) or 25 mm (82 periods, K 1.99, E1 4.59 keV); 4.8/7.0 kW total power at 200 mA; strongbacks rotate 90° with the gap open (FDR Sec. 3-3.3.2).

components.name: Canted undulator front end (CUFE)
components.distanceNote: 19.4 m is the documented position of the CUFE upstream fixed mask (FDR Ch. 3, XBPM1 power table). The front end runs inside the storage-ring tunnel up to the ratchet wall (~24.4 m), with its exit table in 34-ID-A. Model: a schematic train ~15.6-24.0 m (clearing magnet, LPPS, ring valve, burn-through mask, fixed mask at 19.4 m, XBPM1, photon shutter, two safety shutters, differential pumps) in the FDR Ch. 3 order; positions other than the 19.4 m mask are illustrative. The 418 W/mm² rating of that mask is an FDR design case (SCU source), not an ATOMIC operating value.
components.plain: The gatekeeper between accelerator and beamline. Inside the tunnel's concrete wall it can stop both beams in an instant, measures where they point and soaks up kilowatts of unwanted heat, with no window that would spoil the beam's laser-like quality.
components.expert: 2 × 10 kW, 280 kW/mrad² rated; clearing magnet, LPPS, Storage Ring Valve, BTFM1, fixed masks, GRID XBPM1, photon and safety shutters; windowless with differential pumping for 34-ID.

components.name: Front-end exit mask with XBPM2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A thick copper block with two 2-millimetre square holes, one for each twin beam. Only the bright core of each beam gets through into the first hutch.
components.expert: Standard canted front-end exit mask, two 2 × 2 mm² apertures 1 mrad apart; XBPM2 integrated.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A tungsten block that stops stray, very high-energy radiation from the accelerator that travels along with the X-rays.
components.expert: Standard canted front-end exit collimator, 2 × (5 × 5 mm²) apertures; narrowed to help bremsstrahlung management with small-offset monochromators.

components.name: White-beam slits S1 (inboard, 34ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (PDR: ~27 m).
components.plain: Tungsten-edged jaws that trim ATOMIC's beam. Closed down, they act as a tiny new 'source', so only the most laser-like part of the light continues: the first step in making the beam coherent.
components.expert: Canted-undulator variable-aperture photon absorber with tungsten edge inserts. Functions as the primary spatial-coherence selection aperture (S1) - can be closed to form a secondary source or opened to pass a partially coherent beam (PDR).

components.name: Tungsten bremsstrahlung collimator (34ID-BC-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A tungsten radiation shield with clearance holes for both beams; it blocks gamma rays from the ring that would otherwise follow the X-rays down the line.
components.expert: Tungsten collimator.

components.name: Lead bremsstrahlung collimator (34ID-BC-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A lead shield right behind the tungsten one, catching the rest of the stray radiation around the two beam paths.
components.expert: Lead collimator.

components.name: 3DMN outboard white-beam mirror (34ID-MR-1) - partner
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: 3DMN's twin of ATOMIC's mirror bends the neighbouring beam the other way, away from the ring. After the two mirrors the twin beams separate by about 13 milliradians.
components.expert: Flat, horizontally deflecting, 3.0 mrad grazing (6 mrad deflection) toward the outboard side; Si/Rh/Pt stripes (FDR Sec. 4-9.4; PDR Sec. 6-3.4.1). ATOMIC passes ~30 mm inboard of it. Context only.

components.name: Inboard white-beam mirror (34ID-MR-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (PDR: 31 m). The 3DMN outboard mirror sits at 29.6 m.
components.plain: A super-flat silicon mirror struck at a grazing angle of 0.17 degrees. It bends ATOMIC's beam toward the ring, away from its twin, and throws away X-ray energies that are too high. Three stripes (silicon, rhodium, platinum) choose which energies to keep.
components.expert: Flat, horizontally deflecting, 3.0 mrad grazing (6 mrad deflection), notch design to reduce thermal deformation, three stripes (bare Si, Rh, Pt) selected by vertical translation for harmonic rejection. Deflects INBOARD (toward the ring): FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic and PDR Sec. 6-3.4.1 (one mirror outboard for 3DMN, one inboard for ATOMIC). Derived critical energies at 3.0 mrad: Si ~10 keV, Rh ~22 keV, Pt ~28 keV.

components.name: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator (34ID-SC-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (branch not stated; follows the ATOMIC mirror, by analogy with SC-1 after the 3DMN mirror).
components.plain: A lead shield just after ATOMIC's mirror. It catches radiation that went straight on instead of bouncing, so only the mirror-reflected beam travels downstream.
components.expert: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator.

components.name: Diagnostic flag (34ID-BD-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A glowing screen that staff can drop into the beam to see exactly where it is.
components.expert: Diagnostic flag.

components.name: Pink photon mask / white-beam stop (34ID-PM-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: The end of the road for unwanted light: a heavy block that absorbs the straight-through 'white' beams and lets only the two mirror-cleaned 'pink' beams pass.
components.expert: Pink photon mask / white-beam stop; downstream of here only mirror-reflected pink beams propagate.

components.name: Shielded transport 34-ID-A to 34-ID-B (34ID-ST-1)
components.distanceNote: Spans 36.0-42.5 m (FDR Table 4.63; existing white-beam shielded transport reused).
components.plain: A lead-jacketed pipe that carries both beams safely across 6.5 metres of open floor to the next hutch.
components.expert: Existing WB shielded transport.

components.name: Inboard pink-beam photon mask (34ID-PM-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (outboard PM-3 for 3DMN at the same position).
components.plain: A metal aperture that trims the edges of ATOMIC's beam before it enters the optics hutch.
components.expert: Photon mask (inboard, pink beam).

components.name: Lead collimator / bremsstrahlung stop (34ID-BC-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A last lead shield with two small holes. It stops any remaining high-energy radiation before the optics hutch, so people can work safely nearby.
components.expert: Lead collimator / bremsstrahlung stop.

components.name: Beam position monitor (34ID-BD-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: A beam position monitor that reports where the beam is to within micrometres, so it can be held rock-steady on a crystal far downstream.
components.expert: BPM (inboard, Atomic).

components.name: Coherence-defining slits S2 (34ID-SL-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (PDR: ~51 m).
components.plain: A second pair of adjustable jaws, 24 metres after the first. Together the two openings pick out the most laser-like part of the beam, the light that makes sharp speckle patterns.
components.expert: Secondary spatial-coherence selection aperture; with S1 it selects from a single coherent mode up to several modes per plane depending on energy (PDR); also the entrance aperture for the zoom KB1 (PDR).

components.name: Horizontal small-offset double-crystal monochromator (34ID-MN-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (PDR: 51.5 m; FDR Fig. 4.58 drawing shows the chamber at ~51.5-52.2 m, approx).
components.plain: Two perfect silicon crystals pick out a single X-ray colour, essential for clean speckle patterns. The crystals can slide out of the way so the full 'pink' rainbow beam passes for quick orientation pictures; a gently heated second crystal keeps both beams on the same spot.
components.expert: Horizontally deflecting Si(111) DCM, 5.3-30 keV, very small offset (~1.1 mm), pink-beam bypass; second crystal heated (typ. ~60 K above the first) to tune its lattice spacing so the mono beam overlaps the pink-beam path at the sample. Si(111) bandwidth gives ~0.5 µm longitudinal coherence at 10 keV (PDR). Horizontal deflection with a horizontally polarized source makes the beam π-polarized for the crystals: the dynamical Darwin width (and hence bandwidth-integrated throughput) scales as |cos 2θ_B|, ~0.72 at 5.3 keV and ~0.92 at 10 keV (derived; the kinematic cos² factor, 0.52/0.85, overstates the loss for perfect Si).

components.name: 3DMN small-offset DCM (34ID-MN-2) - partner
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (3DMN BPM 52.7 m and slits 53.1 m precede it; not drawn).
components.plain: 3DMN's own crystal monochromator shares the optics hutch with ATOMIC's. Most of the time it stands aside, because 3DMN's signature method uses the full rainbow beam.
components.expert: Horizontally deflecting Si(111) HDCM with pink-beam bypass, ~0.35 m outboard of the ATOMIC beam here. Context only; see the 3DMN exhibit.

components.name: Zoom KB pair 1 (bendable, 34ID-MR-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR text ('first KB pair... in station C at 54 m'), FDR Fig. 4.58 drawing and PDR Table 6.5 all give ~54 m; FDR Table 4.63 lists 52.0 m; FDR Fig. 4.64 ray-trace source-to-mirror distances are 52.7-53.2 m (probably measured from the undulator rather than the straight centre). Use ~54 m in the layout frame.
components.plain: The first half of a mirror 'zoom lens': two 35-centimetre mirrors that bend by 2 to 20 micrometres, less than a hair's width, to focus the beam to an intermediate spot. Sliding that spot back and forth over the next 15 metres changes the final beam size.
components.expert: Two bendable mirrors (H and V), 350 mm long, 3 mrad (up to 5 mrad) incidence; image distance q1 tunable ~1.25-14.3 m (FDR Fig. 4.64), forming the secondary source for KB2; prefigured to an optimal profile and bent both ways; <1 nm rms figure error. PDR: precision apodizing apertures between the pairs to clean the intermediate focus. Model: H mirror centred at 53.75 m and V mirror at 54.25 m (the ray-trace 0.5 m spacing, shifted to the drawing frame); deflections drawn V upward and H inboard (senses not documented). The animated envelope between KB1 and KB2 shows the intermediate focus sliding over the documented q1 range (lateral scale exaggerated ~30×).

specs.deflection: pair deflects in both planes (H mirror first at ~52.7 m, V mirror at ~53.2 m in the ray-trace frame; deflection senses not documented)

components.name: Pink-beam shutter (inboard, 34ID-SH-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (3DMN SH-2 at the same position).
components.plain: A safety door for X-rays. It closes ATOMIC's beam whenever someone enters the experiment hutch, while the neighbouring 3DMN beam keeps running.
components.expert: Pink beam shutter (inboard, Atomic), at the downstream wall of 34-ID-C.

components.name: Shielded pipe through 34-ID-E (34ID-ST-2)
components.distanceNote: Spans 55.1-67.5 m (FDR Table 4.63); FDR Fig. 4.58 shows it ~0.4 m inboard of the 3DMN beam with periodic supports (approx).
components.plain: ATOMIC's beam crosses the whole 3DMN hutch inside this 12-metre lead-shielded pipe, so researchers can work beside it while both experiments run.
components.expert: Shielded pipe to deliver beam to the Atomic endstation 34-ID-F; ATOMIC and 3DMN operate independently.

components.name: 3DMN micro- and nano-diffraction stations (34-ID-E) - partner
components.distanceNote: Micro station ~60.0-60.1 m and nano station ~65.5-65.6 m (FDR Table 4.63 / 3DMN dossier); drawn as ghosted silhouettes.
components.plain: ATOMIC's beam runs right past 3DMN's two experiments, a micro station and a nano station inside its own temperature-stable glass room. Both beamlines can run at the same time.
components.expert: 3DMN micro-diffraction (KB at 60.0 m) and nano-diffraction (KB at 65.5 m, thermal enclosure ~64-66.7 m) instruments; ATOMIC's shielded pipe (55.1-67.5 m) runs ~0.4 m inboard of the 3DMN beam and, per FDR Fig. 4.58, through the nano footprint. Context only; see the 3DMN exhibit.

components.name: End-station beam pre-conditioning platform (BPM, apodizing apertures)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 lists 'K-B Mirror (Atomic) 34ID-MR-4' at 68.1 m; PDR places BPM2 at 68 m. Exact contents of the 'End-station Beam Pre-conditioning Platform' (FDR 4-9.9.2) are not published; BPM/apertures here are inferred from the PDR.
components.plain: A stable table at the hutch entrance carrying the last beam monitors and clean-up apertures, which tidy the beam before the final mirrors.
components.expert: FDR lists an 'End-station Beam Pre-conditioning Platform' as part of the ATOMIC instrument; PDR: BPM2 (68 m), apodizing slits near the intermediate focus (removing slit-diffraction side lobes that otherwise reduce fringe visibility), granite/air-bearing stages for repositioning KB2 when incidence angles change.

components.name: Zoom KB pair 2 (final focusing, 34ID-MR-4)
components.distanceNote: Derived: sample at 69.5 m (FDR Table 4.63) minus FDR Fig. 4.64 image distances (H mirror centre 0.12 m, V mirror centre 0.4 m upstream of focus) → mirror centres ~69.1-69.4 m. FDR Table 4.63 lists the Atomic KB at 68.1 m; FDR text '69 m'; PDR 69 m. Note: the table's 68.1 m coincides with the ray-trace KB2V centre (~68.0-68.15 m, Fig. 4.64, where the implied focus is ~68.4 m), so Table 4.63 appears to mix the ray-trace frame (KB2) with the drawing frame (instrument 69.5 m).
components.plain: The second half of the zoom lens, just in front of the sample: two curved mirrors 40 and 14 centimetres long. Depending on how KB1 is bent, they squeeze the beam to anything from 2 micrometres down to 50 nanometres, about a thousandth of a hair's width.
components.expert: Bendable KB; final H mirror 140 mm (q = 0.12 m, ~50 mm working distance), final V mirror 400 mm (q = 0.4 m); object distance p2 ~1.26-13.7 m set by KB1, which changes the illuminated length and hence the numerical aperture (diffraction-limited FWHM ~0.44 λ/NA for a uniformly filled 1D aperture → NA ~1.25 mrad for 50 nm at 8.7 keV, i.e. ~2.5 mrad full convergence, matching the PDR's ~2.3 × 2.5 mrad; derived). Order along the beam: V mirror (400 mm, centre 0.4 m from focus) then H mirror (140 mm, centre 0.12 m from focus, downstream end ~50 mm from focus). PDR concept based on Matsuyama et al. (SPring-8 zoom 100-1400 nm), optimized analytically for APS-U by Shi et al. 2017; APS prototype (1-D, vertical only: a mechanical bender mirror plus an 18-channel bimorph mirror, tested at 1-BM-B with a grating interferometer) demonstrated zoom at a fixed focal position but only 3.2-10.5 µm FWHM spots, limited by mirror figure error (4.6 nm rms on M1), bending range and the short mirror separation. Model: V mirror 68.9-69.3 m, H mirror 69.31-69.45 m, focus (sample) at 69.5 m.

components.name: Sample-positioning diffractometer (34ID-BI-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 ('Atomic Endstation Instrument'); FDR Fig. 4.58 instrument footprint ~68.8-70.5 m (approx); PDR 69.05 m.
components.plain: The design calls for a massive granite platform and a precision turntable that hold the crystal, turn it to the exact angle at which it reflects, and keep it inside a beam narrower than a virus while it rotates.
components.expert: FDR: separate sample- and detector-positioning diffractometers. PDR concept: granite platform carrying final optics and sample stages, mechanically decoupled from the detector arm (ESRF ID01 model); 3-axis goniometer with tens-of-nm stability over ~1 h scans (R&D on an inverted-joystick hemispherical goniometer); low-profile flexure XYZ stages (mm range, nm steps, fly-scan capable, >1 kg load); beam-sample registration via diamond XBPMs/interferometry. The Beamline Directory currently describes a five-circle diffractometer (3 sample + 2 detector circles), apparently the 34-ID-C heritage instrument. Model: granite block 68.8-70.0 m carrying KB2 and the sample tower; detector circle mounted separately on the floor (PDR concept).

specs.stability: tens of nm over ~1 h (PDR goal)

components.name: Sample goniometer and nanopositioning stages
components.distanceNote: At the focus (approx, = instrument position).
components.plain: Fine motors and piezo stages that rock the crystal through a scan in steps of thousandths of a degree and centre it in the beam to within nanometres.
components.expert: Pre-upgrade 34-ID-C stack (likely heritage): θ air-bearing rotation ±180°, φ/χ circle segments ±17°, coarse XY 25 mm, Z 14 mm, piezo XYZ 100/100/25 µm, Thorlabs KBT1x1 kinematic mount, visible-light confocal microscope for sample finding. As-built ATOMIC stack not published.

components.name: Operando sample environments
components.distanceNote: On the sample stages (approx.). Drawn: a gas-flow heater dome mounted around the sample.
components.plain: Tiny ovens, coolers, liquid cells and working coin-cell batteries, so a crystal can be imaged while it is heated, cooled, charged or bathed in gas. Shown here: a gas-flow heater dome around the sample.
components.expert: Heating chamber with gas flow (RT-900 °C), cryo chamber (>RT to 80 K), RT liquid flow with peristaltic pump, RGA for gas analysis, coin-cell holder for operando batteries (BioLogic SP300); 34-ID-C also had a Linkam-based cryostage, AMPIX cell holder and 70 cfm toxic-gas exhaust.

components.name: Laue orientation detector (Eiger 500K)
components.distanceNote: Close to the sample (at 34-ID-C ~25 mm from focus, on the inboard side facing outboard, movable vertically and inboard/outboard; Zhang et al. 2023); Pateras et al. 2020 used an ASI Timepix GaAs detector 26 mm from the centre of rotation, above and inboard of the beam. Position at 34-ID-F not published: drawn as at 34-ID-C, on the inboard side facing outboard at beam height, sensor face ~28 mm from the sample and centred 30 mm downstream so that it catches forward-scattered Laue spots and clears KB2 (approx.).
components.plain: A camera parked a few centimetres from the sample. When the full rainbow beam hits the crystal it records a starburst of spots that reveals exactly how the crystal is turned, so scientists know where to look for each reflection.
components.expert: Eiger(2) 500K, 1024 × 512 pixels, 75 µm; Zhang et al. quote ~4.7 sr at 25 mm using A/d², which overestimates; the exact solid angle of a centred 76.8 × 38.4 mm² sensor at 25 mm is ~2.1 sr (derived); used only for pink-beam Laue indexing.

components.name: Fluorescence detector
components.distanceNote: Near the sample (approx.). Drawn on the outboard side at 90° to the beam in the horizontal plane, where elastic scattering of the horizontally polarized beam is weakest (illustrative position).
components.plain: A detector that counts the characteristic X-ray 'colours' each element gives off, confirming what the crystal is made of. It looks at the sample from the side, where scattered X-rays are weakest.
components.expert: Listed in the 34-ID-F directory entry; 34-ID-C used a Vortex EX-60 SDD.

components.name: Detector-positioning diffractometer (detector arm)
components.distanceNote: Pivot at the sample (69.5 m); arm ~4.5 m (PDR Fig. 6.7 label '4500'); FDR Fig. 4.58 draws the arm in plan view at ~35° toward the outboard side with a floor arc of radius ~4.1-4.3 m spanning ~8-67° (approx.). Model: boom 4.4 m, posed at δ = 30° (horizontal, outboard) and γ = 16.8° (vertical), i.e. 2θ = 34.0° (Au 111 at 9 keV); the as-built arm geometry is not published.
components.plain: A motorised arm more than 4 metres long that swings around the sample and lifts the camera to wherever the crystal's reflection goes, at distances of up to about 5 metres.
components.expert: Two-circle detector arm independent of the sample platform; detector distance up to ~5 m sufficient because single-view BCDI is limited to ≤1.5-2 µm objects (larger via ptychography) (PDR). Higher-order reflections (e.g. Au 333/400 at 12 keV) need 2θ ~60-80° (PDR). Heritage 34-ID-C arm: δ (rotation about the vertical axis, i.e. horizontal scattering) -2 to 45°, γ (rotation about a horizontal axis, i.e. vertical scattering) -2 to 150°, detector distance 0.5-2.5 m. Because the beam is horizontally polarized, vertical scattering avoids the cos²(2θ) intensity loss at high angles. PDR elevation shows a taller roof for this hutch. Model pose: δ 30°, γ 16.8° → 2θ 34.0° (Au 111, 9 keV); boom 4.4 m with a far-end leg on a floor arc rail of radius ~4.2 m (FDR Fig. 4.58).

components.name: Evacuated flight tube
components.distanceNote: Between sample and BCDI detector along the diffracted beam (used at 34-ID-C). Model: tube from 0.35 m to 2.85 m along the diffracted ray (2θ = 34°); 70.8 m is the along-beam position of its midpoint (illustrative; presence and length on the ATOMIC arm not published).
components.plain: An evacuated pipe between sample and camera. Without air in the way, the faint speckles arrive unblurred.
components.expert: Used at 34-ID-C for ~1 m sample-detector distances; presence/length on the ATOMIC arm not published.

components.name: BCDI photon-counting area detector
components.distanceNote: PDR Table 6.5 'DET 72-75 m'; in practice ~0.1-5 m from the sample at angle 2θ_B off the direct beam (PDR; Zhang et al. 2023). Model: 3.0 m from the sample at 2θ = 34.0° (δ 30° outboard, γ 16.8° up), i.e. ~72.0 m along the beam, 1.45 m outboard and 0.87 m above the beam.
components.plain: A photon-counting camera that registers single X-rays in each pixel. It records the 3D speckle pattern of one reflection while the crystal is rocked; a computer turns that pattern into a 3D image of the crystal and its strain.
components.expert: Directory lists a Timepix-based 512 × 512, 55 µm detector ('TimePix2'); 34-ID-C workhorse was an ASI Quad Timepix with GaAs sensor (~100 Hz, ~11,800 ph/pixel/read). Required distance: D ≥ σ p s / λ (e.g. 0.11 m for 50 nm and 3.4 m for 1.5 µm at 12 keV with 75 µm pixels, 3 px per fringe; PDR). Count rate is a bottleneck: the PDR worst case - the unattenuated, transmitted 50 nm beam spread over a 75 µm-pixel detector at 0.2 m - gives ~7 × 10¹⁰ ph/s/pixel vs ~3 × 10⁶ ph/s/pixel linear limit for Eiger-class detectors; Bragg peaks are far weaker but their central speckle can still saturate (PDR). APS-U detector purchases were descoped.

specs.type: 'TimePix2 512 × 512 55 µm pixel' (directory; vendor not stated - 34-ID-C used ASI Quad Timepix GaAs)

components.name: Pink beam stop (inboard, 34ID-BS-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.plain: The end of the line: a heavy block that safely absorbs whatever beam is left, 78.7 metres from the source.
components.expert: Pink beam stop, inboard; end of the ATOMIC beam.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-A
enclosures.role: First optics enclosure (white beam), shared by ATOMIC and 3DMN
enclosures.notes: Boundaries read from the FDR Fig. 4.58 scale (± ~0.3 m); downstream wall ~35.9-36.0 m (shielded transport ST-1 starts at 36.0 m, FDR Table 4.63). Contains FE exit table, both CUFE white-beam slits, W/Pb collimators, both flat mirrors (3DMN 29.6 m, ATOMIC 31.3 m), secondary collimators, flag and the pink mask / WB stop (34.0 m). The inboard side is the angled storage-ring shield wall.

enclosures.name: Transport
enclosures.role: No hutch: the shielded white-beam pipe 34ID-ST-1 crosses the experiment floor

instruments.name: ATOMIC coherent-imaging endstation (FDR design)
instruments.plain: A super-stable stage holds and rotates a single micro- or nano-crystal in a zoomable X-ray spot while a camera on a long arm records the speckle pattern from one of its reflections. A computer then rebuilds a 3D map of the crystal and of how its atoms are displaced.

instruments.expert: Upstream instrument on the outboard canted beam (3.0 cm undulator, LN2-cooled flat Pt mirror at 5 mrad, ~17 keV practical maximum); small-offset (1 mm) movable Si(111) DCM on an air-bearing granite stage (6-20 keV) enabling pink/mono switching; bendable KB focusing to ~0.5 × 0.7 µm (H × V), sample at 7 cm from the H mirror; slitted unfocused beam ~30 × 70 µm; sample stack θ (air bearing) + φ/χ + XYZ + piezo; detector arm δ (horizontal) -2 to 45°, γ (vertical) -2 to 150°, 0.5-2.5 m; detectors ASI Timepix (Si, GaAs; a GaAs Timepix also served as the Laue detector in 2020), Eiger2 500K for Laue by 2023; confocal microscope; sample environments for gas, heat, cryo, liquids, batteries. geometryNotes: Canted pair in the sector-34 straight: ATOMIC is the DOWNSTREAM undulator (revolver U21/U25) and the INBOARD beam, 1.0 mrad from the 3DMN U28 beam (upstream/outboard) (FDR). This reverses the pre-upgrade assignment, when the coherent-imaging station 34-ID-C took the outboard beam and deflected it a further 10 mrad outboard (34-ID wiki, 2013). All hutches sit on the existing experiment floor within the sector footprint (no long-beamline building). Order along the beam (FDR naming): 34-ID-A FOE ~24.4-36.0 m → shielded transport 36.0-42.5 m → 34-ID-B ~42.3-47.8 m → 34-ID-C ~47.8-55.0 m (optics, ex-BCDI station) → 34-ID-E 55.0-67.5 m (3DMN; ATOMIC in a shielded pipe ~0.4 m inboard of the 3DMN beam, approx.) → 34-ID-F 67.5-~79.8 m (new ATOMIC hutch). Boundaries re-measured on the FDR Fig. 4.58 scale bar (~25 px/m) and harmonized with the 3DMN dossier; the C/E wall is constrained to ~55.0 m by the shutters (54.8 m) and the start of the shielded pipe (55.1 m). Naming changed between PDR 2017 (SOE '34-ID-B', 3DMN '34-ID-D', ATOMIC '34-ID-E') and FDR 2019 (C = optics, E = 3DMN, F = ATOMIC). Deflections: the ATOMIC flat mirror (31.3 m) reflects horizontally at 3.0 mrad grazing (6 mrad deflection) toward the ring (INBOARD), as drawn in the FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic and stated in the PDR (one mirror outboard for 3DMN, one inboard for ATOMIC, ~11 mrad between the pink beams at the PDR's 2.5 mrad; ~13 mrad at 3.0 mrad, derived) - consistent with the ~0.4 m beam separation seen in 34-ID-E in Fig. 4.58; the HDCM deflects horizontally with only ~1.1 mm lateral offset (no vertical offset), so the mono beam is laterally shifted ~1 mm, not raised; the zoom KB pairs deflect in both planes by ~6 mrad each (3 mrad grazing; up to 10 mrad at 5 mrad incidence), so the beam axis at the sample is tilted slightly (sense not documented). Beam height: APS standard ~1.4 m above floor (consistent with the PDR elevation; approx). In 34-ID-F (FDR Fig. 4.58, approx.): the beam runs ~2 m from the straight inboard wall; the hutch is ~7.5 m wide at its upstream wall and narrows along a diagonal outboard wall (with a step near ~74.8 m) to ~2 m at ~79.8 m; diffractometer ~69.5-69.7 m; a ~4.5 m detector arm (PDR label '4500'; the FDR Fig. 4.58 arc has a radius of ~4.2-4.4 m) is drawn in plan view sweeping toward the wide outboard side (a plan view cannot show vertical travel); the PDR elevation shows a taller roof here (~3.5 m) than the upstream hutches (~2.6 m) for vertical detector travel; pink beam stop at 78.7 m. Distance inconsistencies: KB1 52.0 m (FDR table) vs 54 m (FDR text, FDR/PDR drawings) vs 52.7-53.2 m (FDR ray-trace frame); KB2 68.1 m (table) vs ~69.1-69.4 m implied by 0.12/0.4 m image distances and a 69.5 m sample - the ray-trace frame appears ~1.1 m shorter (likely measured from the downstream undulator, not the straight centre). For a 3D model use the drawing frame: KB1 ~54 m, KB2 immediately upstream of a 69.5 m sample, working distance ~50 mm. Polarization: the undulator beam is linearly polarized in the horizontal plane. Grazing-incidence mirrors are essentially polarization-insensitive; the horizontally deflecting Si(111) DCM passes π-polarization, so its bandwidth/throughput scales as |cos 2θ_B| (~0.72 at 5.3 keV, ~0.92 at 10 keV, derived); for scattering from the sample in the horizontal plane the kinematic intensity factor is cos²(2θ) (0.69 for Au 111 at 9 keV, ~0.25-0.02 at 2θ = 60-80°), which is why the heritage 34-ID-C arm reached high angles mainly vertically (γ up to 150° vs δ up to 45° horizontally).

interactiveIdeas.title: Strain you can see: from speckle to 3D displacement
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors deform a cartoon nanocrystal (squeeze a corner, insert a dislocation, adsorb molecules on a facet). Beside it, a live 2D/3D Bragg-peak speckle pattern updates; a perfect crystal gives a symmetric pattern, strain makes it lopsided. A 'reconstruct' button runs a few hundred ER/HIO iterations in the browser and colours the recovered crystal by phase = displacement along G.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: BCDI images shape (amplitude) and atomic displacement (phase) at once; symmetric peaks mean no strain; it is the asymmetry that encodes strain.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: I(q) = |FT{ρ(r) exp(i G·u(r))}|² around q = G; phase φ = G·u, so for Au(111) (d = 2.355 Å) 1 rad = d/2π = 0.375 Å displacement (wraps every 2.355 Å); strain ε_zz = (1/|G|) dφ/dz. Bragg angle λ = 2 d sin(θ): Au(111) at 9 keV → 2θ = 34.0°. Oversampling ≥ 2 per dimension (fringe spacing λ D / s; e.g. 300 nm crystal, 9 keV, 1.1 m → ~505 µm = ~9 pixels of 55 µm). Phase retrieval has trivial ambiguities (global phase, twin/conjugate inversion, translation). A rocking scan of ~0.3-1° samples the third dimension. Real BCDI resolution today ~10-30 nm; do not show atoms unless in the 'future' mode.

interactiveIdeas.title: A zoom lens made of mirrors
interactiveIdeas.concept: A side-view of the 15-m-long two-stage KB system. A slider bends KB1 so its intermediate focus slides from just after KB1 to just before KB2; the beam footprint on KB2, the numerical aperture and the final spot (50 nm to 2 µm) update live, together with flux and a 'sample size' that the spot should match.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Zoom optics change the size of a focused coherent beam without moving the focus; small spots need a large illuminated aperture on the last mirror; matching spot to sample wastes no coherent photons.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Geometry from FDR Fig. 4.64: KB1 350 mm mirrors at p1 ~53 m; KB1→KB2 ~15 m; KB2 H 140 mm with q2 = 0.12 m (50 mm working distance), V 400 mm with q2 = 0.4 m; all at 3 mrad grazing (footprint = beam size / θ, so 350 mm accepts ~1 mm). Coherent illumination → spot is diffraction-limited: FWHM ~0.44 λ/NA for a uniformly filled 1D aperture, with NA ~ (illuminated length × θ)/(2 q2); 50 nm at 8.7 keV needs NA ~1.25 mrad (derived), within reach of KB2H (140 mm × 3 mrad / (2 × 0.12 m) = 1.75 mrad max) and KB2V (400 mm × 3 mrad / (2 × 0.4 m) = 1.5 mrad max); PDR: ~2.3 × 2.5 mrad divergence for 50 nm, ~65 × 70 µrad for 1.5 µm. Geometric source image M = (q1/p1)(q2/p2) is smaller than the diffraction limit at 50 nm, so do not model the small end as source demagnification. Figure error must be <1 nm rms. Flux values: 3.1 × 10¹² (50 nm) vs 4.6 × 10¹² ph/s/0.1%BW (2 µm) at 8.7 keV.

interactiveIdeas.title: Flashlight vs laser: coherence before and after the upgrade
interactiveIdeas.concept: Two electron-beam cross-sections (old 280 × 10 µm rms vs new 14.7 × 3.2 µm) launch wavefronts down a 50 m beamline; a double-slit or nanocrystal at the end shows fringe visibility. Visitors close the S1/S2 slits to filter coherence and watch flux drop vs visibility rise.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Only the coherent part of the beam makes sharp speckle; APS-U makes the beam ~100× more coherent at ~10 keV so the slits throw away far fewer photons.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Total photon source Σ = √(σe² + σr²), Σ' = √(σe'² + σr'²), σr = √(2 λ L)/4π, σr' = √(λ/2L), L = 2.1 m; coherent fraction per plane = (λ/4π)/(Σ Σ'): ~0.11 (H) × 0.48 (V) at 10 keV for APS-U brightness mode vs ~0.003 × 0.16 before (derived from FDR Table 1.1). Transverse coherence length at distance z ~ λ z/(2 π Σ) (one common convention; ~70 µm H at 50 m, 10 keV, APS-U vs ~3.5 µm before). Longitudinal coherence λ²/(2 Δλ) ~0.5 µm at 10 keV for Si(111) (PDR) - path differences across the crystal must stay below this. Coherent flux at 20 keV up ~520× (FDR Table 1.1).

interactiveIdeas.title: The photon budget for seeing atoms
interactiveIdeas.concept: A resolution slider from 30 nm to 0.2 nm shows how far out in reciprocal space the detector must see, how fast the speckle intensity falls, and the dose and beam time needed - with the old APS, APS-U, and a 'radiation damage / heating' warning light.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Resolution is limited by how many photons you can collect at high scattering angles, not by lenses; atomic resolution is a photon (and detector, and sample-survival) problem that APS-U makes approachable.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Half-period resolution ~π/q_max (2π/q_max is the smallest lattice period sampled; e.g. q_max = 1.26 Å⁻¹ → ~2.5 Å half-period); for a compact object the speckle envelope falls ~q⁻⁴ (Porod), so dose rises steeply (roughly as resolution⁻⁴ for fixed signal per voxel); Dietze & Shpyrko: ~10¹⁸ ph/µm² for atomic resolution of a 20 nm Au crystal, ~10¹⁷ for amorphous Au. At 3.1 × 10¹² ph/s in a 50 × 50 nm² spot (1.2 × 10¹⁵ ph/s/µm²) 10¹⁸ ph/µm² takes ~800 s (derived; PDR estimate ~1000 s). Focused power ~8 mW in 50 × 50 nm² at 10 keV (PDR) - sample heating and damage matter. Detector: the unattenuated transmitted 50 nm beam on 75 µm pixels at 0.2 m would be ~7 × 10¹⁰ ph/s/pixel vs ~3 × 10⁶ linear limit (PDR worst case; Bragg-peak speckles are much weaker).

interactiveIdeas.title: Find the crystal: Laue then Bragg
interactiveIdeas.concept: A game: a random sub-micron grain sits on a substrate. Visitors first flash the pink beam to get a Laue starburst on the near detector, click to index it, then swing the detector arm and rock the sample to land the coherent reflection on the far detector, finally choosing three reflections to build the full strain tensor.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why the beamline keeps a pink-beam bypass and a near-sample Laue detector; how orientation finding turns a needle-in-a-haystack search into a few clicks; why three non-coplanar reflections give the full strain tensor.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Pink-beam bandwidth at 34-ID-C ~5-20 keV: every reciprocal-lattice point between the Ewald spheres for E_min and E_max diffracts at once; orientation accuracy ~0.01° possible with known energy calibration; mono beam then aligned with heated second DCM crystal so pink and mono beams share a focus. Each reflection gives u·G_hkl; three non-coplanar G give u(r) and the 6-component strain tensor. Detector 2θ for Au 333/400 at 12 keV is ~60-80° (PDR); horizontal-plane scattering suffers the cos²(2θ) polarization factor in intensity (horizontally polarized beam), so high-angle reflections are better reached by vertical detector motion (34-ID-C γ to 150°).

funFacts: The first 3D image of the strain field inside a single nanocrystal (a lead crystal) was made at 34-ID-C - ATOMIC's predecessor - and published in Nature in 2006.

The name is aspirational: the beamline's designer describes 'Atomic' as meant to be inspirational, asking whether coherent X-ray imaging can finally reach wavelength-limited (atomic) resolution. It began as APS-U white paper WP28 in January 2016.

In the FDR design, the old coherent-imaging hutch 34-ID-C becomes an optics hutch holding ATOMIC's monochromator and the first half of its zoom lens, while the new experiment hutch 34-ID-F was built at the end of the line.
ATOMIC and its twin 3DMN start from the same 5-m-long straight section; their beams leave the front end just 1 milliradian apart - about 2.5 cm apart after 25 m (derived).
ATOMIC's undulator is a 'revolver': two magnet arrays (21 and 25 mm periods) on a strongback that rotates 90 degrees to swap them.

The zoom mirrors must keep their shape errors below 1 nanometre rms - a few atoms high - along mirrors up to 40 cm long, even while being bent. (The PDR, discussing an ultra-stable hemispherical goniometer, notes for comparison that the Hubble Space Telescope mirror's figure error is about 30 nm.)

If the full, unattenuated 50-nm beam passed straight through a sample onto a detector 20 cm away, each 75-micron pixel would receive about 7 × 10¹⁰ photons per second - roughly 20,000 times what an Eiger-class pixel can count linearly (PDR worst case).
ATOMIC is expected to produce 250-300 terabytes of data a year, about 400 times more than its predecessor 34-ID-C (~0.65 TB/yr).
Focused into 50 × 50 nm, the beam carries about 8 milliwatts - so for the first time, keeping the sample from heating up becomes part of the experiment design.
BCDI displacement maps are sensitive to shifts of a small fraction of an atomic spacing: a 2017 Science study of a heated gold film reached 10-nm spatial and sub-angstrom displacement resolution.

openQuestions: As-built endstation hardware is not publicly documented: diffractometer vendor/geometry, whether the 34-ID-C five-circle instrument was moved to 34-ID-F (the directory text suggests so), detector-arm length/angular ranges, and whether the PDR 'inverted-joystick' ultra-stable goniometer was ever built. Also unknown: whether the new arm scatters mainly vertically (preferred for a horizontally polarized beam, as at 34-ID-C) or horizontally as the FDR plan view suggests.

Zoom KB as built: bender vs bimorph technology, whether both pairs are installed and commissioned, and the measured spot range. The only published hardware test (2020 1-BM prototype) reached micron-scale spots limited by figure error; AutoFocus (2023) used the 34-ID-C KB digital twin.

Component positions: ATOMIC KB1 at 52.0 m (FDR Table 4.63) vs 54 m (FDR text and drawings) vs 52.7-53.2 m (FDR ray trace); KB2 68.1 m (table) vs ~69.1-69.4 m implied by the 69.5 m instrument position and 0.12/0.4 m image distances. Exact sample position (68.4 m ray-trace frame vs 69.5 m table) unconfirmed.

Detectors in use at 34-ID-F in 2026: directory lists a 'TimePix2' 512 × 512 / 55 µm detector and an Eiger 500K for Laue only; APS-U detector purchases were descoped (2024). No evidence found for a Lambda detector at ATOMIC; whether an Eiger2 4M/500K or other high-rate detector is used for BCDI is unknown.

Status: stage 5 (scientific commissioning/early experiments) on 2026-10-05 and listed for GU proposals on 2026-10-07, but the date of entry into the general user program (stage 6) and any first post-upgrade ATOMIC publications were not found; the Beamline Directory ('Construction') and Feature Beamlines page ('to come') are stale.

Undulator length: FDR 2.1 m and ID table period counts (98 × 21 mm, 82 × 25 mm) vs Beamline Directory '2.3 m' (possibly overall mechanical length). FDR Table 4.62 power values (763/738 W) and K values (1.939/1.305) are listed in an order that makes their pairing with the 21/25 mm arrays ambiguous.

Monochromator options: directory lists a 'Multilayer Monochromator' entry with no specs; the PDR proposed an optional DMM and a diamond phase plate, neither of which appears in the FDR. Unclear whether either exists at ATOMIC.

Mirror deflection senses: RESOLVED for the white-beam mirror - it deflects inboard (FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic, PDR Sec. 6-3.4.1). Still undocumented: which way each KB mirror deflects, and the exact beam offset/height at the sample.
Hutch outline dimensions (widths, roof height, detector-arm sweep) are read from low-resolution FDR/PDR drawings (± ~0.3 m or worse) and the FDR and PDR outlines differ in detail.

Project scope split: Dec 2024 / Jan 2025 updates said only 'infrastructure' for 3DMN/Atomic would be complete within the APS-U project, while MEDSI 2025 states all nine feature beamlines met their KPPs; which ATOMIC components were delivered by the project vs. operations funding is unclear.

Energy range: 5.3-30 keV (FDR, directory) vs 5-25 keV (PDR); the practical upper limit depends on mirror stripe and harmonic choice and has not been reported from commissioning. Derived: at the 3.0 mrad design angle the Pt-stripe critical energy is ~28 keV, so 30 keV operation through the white-beam mirror and four KB mirrors needs smaller angles or will have low throughput.
Whether pink-beam CDI and Bragg ptychography modes are available to users in 2026.
